bridge: C01 introduced types and memory representation. Use only the supplied local teaching program and invented short strings.
teaching:
### Count positions from zero

An array with five elements has valid indices 0 through 4. Index 5 is already outside it. The number of available elements and the largest valid index are therefore different numbers.

When a program receives a length, ask whether it counts bytes, characters or elements. They can differ. UTF-8 text may use several bytes for one character.

### Leave room for a string terminator

A conventional C string ends with a zero byte called the null terminator. A buffer that stores four visible single-byte characters needs a fifth byte for that terminator. Without a terminator inside the available range, a string-reading function may keep reading past the intended contents.

### Check before copying

A buffer is an area of memory reserved for data. Before writing, compare the required byte count with its capacity using safe arithmetic. Check the return and termination rules of the actual function; a function name containing “safe” is not a complete guarantee.

### Handle boundaries deliberately

Test empty input, an exact fit, one byte too many and multi-byte text. Avoid changing a byte count into a character count without decoding the encoding. A displayed word can look short while needing more storage than the program allowed.
explanation: The comparison rejects a source whose visible byte length leaves no room for the terminator. Copying strlen+1 includes the terminator. This small example assumes src is already a valid terminated string; strlen itself cannot safely validate an arbitrary unterminated buffer.
exercise: Save the example as strings.c. Compile with cc -std=c11 -Wall -Wextra strings.c -o strings, then run ./strings. On the next terminal line, run printf 'status=%s\n' "$?" to display that run’s exit status; run no other command between them. Repeat after changing src to "cats", then to "", recompiling each time. Predict the displayed text and status first. Draw the occupied indices for accepted inputs, including the terminator. The rejected case prints no text; the status is how it reports refusal.
solution: With "cat", the program prints cat and returns status 0; indices 0–3 contain c,a,t and the terminator. With "cats", strlen is 4, so 4>=4 is true and return 1 stops before copying; status is 1. With "", strlen is 0; copying 0+1 byte stores just the terminator at index 0, then printf displays an empty line and the program returns 0. The remaining array bytes are not part of that empty string. None of these cases needs access beyond dst[3].
challenge: A destination has capacity 6 bytes. Decide whether ASCII inputs "hello", "planet" and "" fit as terminated strings. Explain why a five-character Unicode string may still fail this byte-capacity check.
challenge_solution: hello fits exactly with its terminator; planet needs 7 bytes and is rejected; empty needs 1. UTF-8 characters can occupy multiple bytes, so visible character count does not establish byte length.
